title: Monte Testaccio, a 35-metre hill in Rome, is made of tens of millions of broken oil jars
body: Monte Testaccio, near the Tiber in Rome, is an artificial hill about 35 m high and nearly a kilometre round, made almost entirely of broken **amphorae**. Most were Dressel 20s, round jars of about 70 litres that carried olive oil from Baetica in southern Spain; labels painted on them record the jar’s empty weight, the merchant, the weight of the oil and the inspectors. The oil was probably poured into bulk containers at the port, but these jars were not reused: they broke into big curved pieces that were hard to crush for building, and oily clay may have spoiled mortar, since oil and lime make soap. Instead, from Emperor Augustus’s time until about AD 260, the empties were probably carried up on donkeys or mules, smashed, and laid in terraces held by walls of jars packed with sherds, with lime sprinkled against the smell. How many? José Remesal, who co-directs the excavations, estimates something like 25 million, [Archaeology magazine reports](https://archaeology.org/issues/march-april-2009/features/trash-talk/); a figure of 53 million is also cited. At 70 litres a jar, that is some 2 to 4 billion litres of oil, mostly brought in for the state’s food supply.

slides.question: Monte Testaccio is a hill in Rome made almost entirely of broken Roman pottery. About how tall is it?
slides.explanation: About 35 m, and nearly a kilometre round. In Roman times it was probably taller still.

slides.alt: Animation on a bright Roman day: Monte Testaccio, 35 m high and made of sherds; a 70-litre Dressel 20 oil jar shipped from Baetica; its painted labels and weights; oily clay and lime making soap; a donkey carrying jars up terraces of jars and sherds; bars for 25 and 53 million jars.

slides.prompt: Set the jars in the hill to each estimate, 25 million and 53 million, and see how much olive oil each one means.
slides.takeaway: 25 million jars of 70 litres held 1.75 billion litres, 53 million about 3.7 billion. Spread over 250 years, that is roughly 7 to 15 million litres of oil a year.

slides.alt: Monte Testaccio today: a steep hill covered in dry grass, shrubs and pine trees, rising behind low buildings and a car park.

left.label: Many amphorae
left.text: Reused for other goods, or crushed into chips for building concrete.

right.label: These oil jars
right.text: Thick walls broke into big curved pieces, and oily clay may have spoiled mortar.

slides.question: What did the painted labels on Monte Testaccio’s oil jars record?
options: The jar’s weight and the oil’s weight
The buyer’s home address in Rome
The ship’s name and its route
The price the oil sold for
slides.explanation: The labels, tituli picti, give the empty jar’s weight, the merchant, the weight of the oil, the people who weighed it and the farm’s district.
